quiz.question: 1. What defines a monolithic backend most directly?
options: It must run on one physical server
It is deployed as a single application unit
It cannot contain internal modules
quiz.explanation: A monolith is defined strictly by its deployment unit: it is packaged and deployed as a single application unit. It can (and should) have internal modular boundaries, and it can run scaled horizontally across hundreds of servers behind a load balancer.

quiz.question: 2. Which statement best describes a modular monolith?
options: One deployable application with explicit internal module boundaries
A collection of services that always communicate over a network
An application without a database
quiz.explanation: A modular monolith is a single deployable application that enforces explicit internal module boundaries, clear public interfaces, and logical data ownership without incurring distributed network overhead.

quiz.question: 3. What is high cohesion?
options: Every module depends on every other module
Related responsibilities are grouped together within a module
All modules write directly to the same database tables
quiz.explanation: High cohesion means elements that belong together logically and change together for the same business reasons are grouped within the same module boundary.

quiz.question: 4. What is a bounded context?
options: A fixed number of services deployed together
A boundary within which a particular domain model and vocabulary apply
A type of database index
quiz.explanation: In Domain-Driven Design (DDD), a bounded context is the linguistic and conceptual boundary within which a particular domain model and its ubiquitous language hold true unambiguously.

quiz.question: 5. What is a distributed monolith?
options: A well-isolated service architecture with independent releases
Several deployments with tight dependencies that force coordinated changes or cause cascading failures
A monolith replicated behind a load balancer
quiz.explanation: A distributed monolith possesses the operational distribution and complexity of microservices (network latencies, partial failures) combined with the tight coupling of a monolith (shared database schemas, coordinated release trains).

quiz.question: 6. Which signal most strongly supports creating an independent service?
options: A desire to use a fashionable framework
A requirement for a capability to scale and deploy independently, supported by clear boundaries
A preference for more repositories
quiz.explanation: Valid justification requires distinct operational needs: different hardware/scaling characteristics, independent release schedules, or distinct fault-isolation requirements, underpinned by well-defined domain boundaries.

quiz.question: 7. Why can multiple services modifying the same internal database tables be problematic?
options: It necessarily makes all SQL queries slow
It creates unclear data ownership and couples services to each other's schemas
It prevents the use of HTTP
quiz.explanation: Shared database access bypasses service boundaries, couples independent services to internal schema implementations, causes locking contention, and destroys autonomous deployability.

quiz.question: 8. What is the purpose of the Strangler Fig pattern?
options: Replace an entire system in one high-risk rewrite
Incrementally replace selected functionality while the old and new systems coexist
Eliminate all API contracts
quiz.explanation: The Strangler Fig pattern replaces an existing legacy system gradually by placing an intercepting proxy in front and routing specific capabilities to new implementations while both run concurrently.

scenarios.title: How do you decide between a Modular Monolith and Microservices for a new product?
scenarios.context: A startup is launching an AI-powered technical learning platform expecting 50,000 users in Year 1.
scenarios.answer: Default to a Modular Monolith. When domain boundaries are still evolving, refactoring in-memory code across packages is fast and safe. If you premature decompose into microservices, wrong boundaries require refactoring distributed network contracts, data migrations, and dual deployments. Fowler's 'Monolith First' principle applies: start modular, enforce strict interfaces, and only extract when independent scaling or autonomous team boundaries demand it.

scenarios.title: What is the single most common cause of the 'Distributed Monolith' disaster?
scenarios.context: A team split their backend into 8 Docker containers but deploys all 8 every Tuesday together.
scenarios.answer: The shared database anti-pattern. When multiple microservices connect to the same PostgreSQL or MySQL instance and execute SQL joins across each other's tables, they are not independent services. A schema change by Service A breaks Service B at runtime. True microservices require Database-per-Service: private data stores accessible only via the service's published API or asynchronous events.

scenarios.title: How do you maintain data consistency across services without distributed 2PC locking?
scenarios.context: A student pays for a subscription and enrolls in a course. Billing Service and Course Service are separate.
scenarios.answer: Avoid Two-Phase Commit (2PC) because it locks database rows across network hops, causing severe latency and availability bottlenecks. Instead, use the Saga Pattern with Eventual Consistency and the Transactional Outbox. Billing commits the charge and writes a 'PaymentSucceeded' event to its local outbox table atomically. A CDC or relay daemon publishes the event to Kafka. Course Service consumes the event idempotently and provisions the enrollment. If course provisioning fails permanently, a compensating event is dispatched to refund the charge.

scenarios.title: How does Conway's Law govern microservice architecture success?
scenarios.context: 'Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations.'
scenarios.answer: Microservices are fundamentally an organizational scaling pattern, not just a technical one. A team of 5 engineers running 20 microservices experiences immense operational friction because the communication overhead exceeds the cognitive boundary benefits. Conversely, an organization of 200 engineers across 15 autonomous feature teams needs service boundaries to prevent code merge conflicts and deployment bottlenecks. Align service boundaries with cross-functional two-pizza teams.

scenarios.title: How do you safely extract a capability from a live monolith without downtime?
scenarios.context: PrepSpaces needs to extract its CPU-heavy AI Interview Service from the main monolith.
scenarios.answer: Execute the 5-stage Strangler Fig pattern: 1) Refactor the interview code inside the monolith behind a clean TypeScript/Java interface facade. 2) Stand up the new AI Interview service with its own database. 3) Configure an API Gateway/Reverse Proxy to intercept '/api/interviews' routes. 4) Mirror traffic or canary route 5% of traffic to the new service while monitoring error budgets and database sync. 5) Gradually increase to 100%, deprecate the legacy monolithic path, and delete dead code.

scenarios.title: What are Architectural Fitness Functions, and how do they enforce modular boundaries?
scenarios.context: Preventing developers from importing internal classes across module boundaries over time.
scenarios.answer: Fitness functions are automated tests that fail in CI/CD if architectural integrity is violated. In Java, ArchUnit asserts that 'classes in package `course.domain` cannot access classes in `assessment.internal`'. In TypeScript/Node.js, ESLint boundary rules (`import/no-restricted-paths`) or dependency-cruiser prevent illegal cross-module imports. This guarantees that a modular monolith remains modular over years of fast-paced development.
